items.content:
But when does the system decide to monitor a call for 'fraud' you may ask !?
Well, according to the code in the phones 'Ad Guard' and SecurityRisk components, it latches on to calls that are not in the user's phonebook or not matching the 'yellow pages' database. Then a ASR transcriber sets in and it transmits the call's content for classification.
If the call is VoIP from WeChat/QQ it always gets transmitted it seems ( either video or just audio, depending on what is active ). 
It has to be said, that this functionality can be disabled by the user. There is a debug variant of it built in, that doesn't read the 'has agreed to have the calls monitored' flag. But overall it needs the consent of the user to actually work. 
As it was stated in the earlier post, the system also transmits a lot of other details on the user and the connection to Tencent by default. 
And if the story is true, it seems to be able to get directly accessed by the Police's automatic analysis systems. Which results in calls from the law enforcement if illegal app's are used on a phone. 
Technically this feature is emulating exactly what the official anti-fraud app of the Ministry of Public Security released a while back.

items.content:
My father was the lead avonics technician for Leerjet in Tucson for over 20 years, I know he would have had a heavy heart today over these events if he were still alive.  He had a long history of working with aircraft: U2s and C130s (his faves) in the air force during Vietnam, every Leerjets model including their towed missile variants, US customs mbb bo 105 (his least fave) and Blackhawks, and literally Frankenstein custom hand building fire bomber planes made to order for fire fighting.

During his 2 tennures at Leerjet, he took every incident with their aircraft personally. He was a true mcguyver and a lot of his untraditional methods to diagnostic analysis for planes became textbook. Many famous people would request him to look at their planes because they knew we wouldn't stop until it was fixed.

After any incident, I often would find him up 3 am looking over whatever details he could find about it.  He would methodically think how something could go wrong to the point that he incorporated nontraditional fuzzing tools into his work (at the time unheard of in the industry). Before he died he developed a method for fuzzing the diagnostic tools that were used to evaluate the avionics and mechanics of these aircraft to simulate race conditions, "one out of a million bad lucks", and other hard to track issues. 

I know today if he were alive he'd be looking up that flights service record and doing everything he could to ensure what went wrong, they could detect it and try his damndest it didn't ever happen again.

To the 9 souls on board, I hope they are at peace, and their memories are cherished by all of those in their lives.

items.content:
RT @TuckerCarlson: Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one. “Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” says an informed observer.

Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.

To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated settlement to the war they’ve so grievously mismanaged; both are pushing to restart major combat operations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe are also following Netanyahu’s lead, as are leaders of the Democratic Party. In a recent meeting on the subject, former president Barack Obama said he opposes the current Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha.

The rest of America’s longtime allies in the Middle East are terrified by the prospect of more war. On September 27th, Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to enlist the UAE in his lobbying effort for a final attack on Iran. The Emiratis refused. After eight months of conflict, Gulf economies are teetering. So are global energy and fertilizer markets. They won’t recover soon. Globally, there are a total of about 850 supertankers used to transport oil from producers to the rest of the world. In October alone, 11 of them were badly damaged in Hormuz. At this pace, a global depression is imminent. A nuclear strike would radically accelerate the destruction. Fallout from a ground explosion at Pickax Mountain would contaminate the Persian Gulf, poisoning the water supply for 100 million people.

And those are just some of the immediate consequences for the region. The rest of the world is every bit as exposed. No country other than the United States has ever used a nuclear weapon in war. Some would like to. An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final.

We’ve been sleepwalking toward this moment for months. Since February, the administration has quietly rewritten America’s nuclear doctrine to make first use of so-called “battlefield nukes” easier and therefore more likely. No one in Washington in either party seems bothered by this. Now we’re on the brink of it.

Close observers say Trump is likely to decide by next weekend whether or not to use nuclear weapons. That would be November 7, six days from now. To his credit, he’s hesitating. At the moment, Trump is listening to his vice president, JD Vance, and to his envoy and friend Steve Witkoff, both of whom argue a deal with Iran can be made.

They’re right, though it won’t be simple. The Iranians are famously frustrating to negotiate with under any circumstances, and elements of that government have become more radical since Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his family were killed in February. After decades of isolation, even relatively moderate Iranian leaders seem confused by how decisions are made in the West. (There is a widespread belief in Tehran, for example, that the United States government controls Israel.) But overall, people who have spoken to decision-makers in Iran say there is consensus there that more war is bad for everyone and a deal is worth making.

One group that hasn’t been consulted so far is the global population — the hundreds of millions of people who will be killed along with their children if Trump is pushed by Netanyahu into launching a nuclear strike next week. Now would be the time for them to speak up.

After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.

To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated settlement to the war they’ve so grievously mismanaged; both are pushing to restart major combat operations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe are also following Netanyahu’s lead, as are leaders of the Democratic Party. In a recent meeting on the subject, former president Barack Obama said he opposes the current Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha.

The rest of America’s longtime allies in the Middle East are terrified by the prospect of more war. On September 27th, Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to enlist the UAE in his lobbying effort for a final attack on Iran. The Emiratis refused. After eight months of conflict, Gulf economies are teetering. So are global energy and fertilizer markets. They won’t recover soon. Globally, there are a total of about 850 supertankers used to transport oil from producers to the rest of the world. In October alone, 11 of them were badly damaged in Hormuz. At this pace, a global depression is imminent. A nuclear strike would radically accelerate the destruction. Fallout from a ground explosion at Pickax Mountain would contaminate the Persian Gulf, poisoning the water supply for 100 million people.

And those are just some of the immediate consequences for the region. The rest of the world is every bit as exposed. No country other than the United States has ever used a nuclear weapon in war. Some would like to. An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final.

We’ve been sleepwalking toward this moment for months. Since February, the administration has quietly rewritten America’s nuclear doctrine to make first use of so-called “battlefield nukes” easier and therefore more likely. No one in Washington in either party seems bothered by this. Now we’re on the brink of it.

Close observers say Trump is likely to decide by next weekend whether or not to use nuclear weapons. That would be November 7, six days from now. To his credit, he’s hesitating. At the moment, Trump is listening to his vice president, JD Vance, and to his envoy and friend Steve Witkoff, both of whom argue a deal with Iran can be made.

They’re right, though it won’t be simple. The Iranians are famously frustrating to negotiate with under any circumstances, and elements of that government have become more radical since Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his family were killed in February. After decades of isolation, even relatively moderate Iranian leaders seem confused by how decisions are made in the West. (There is a widespread belief in Tehran, for example, that the United States government controls Israel.) But overall, people who have spoken to decision-makers in Iran say there is consensus there that more war is bad for everyone and a deal is worth making.

One group that hasn’t been consulted so far is the global population — the hundreds of millions of people who will be killed along with their children if Trump is pushed by Netanyahu into launching a nuclear strike next week. Now would be the time for them to speak up.

items.content:
RT @S1r1u5_: i think there's a lot more to cybersecurity than finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. we know a huge number of real-world compromises happen through social engineering and other relatively mundane failures.

you could spend an absurd amount of money finding and patching every vulnerability, but what good is that if an attacker can just walk through another door you have left wide open?

you have made the software more secure, but have you actually reduced the risk of compromise?

if only @LiveOverflow had simply said, "'for me', everything outside vulnerability research is boring. I enjoy finding and exploiting bugs, building mitigations and defenses, and i am not particularly interested in the broader ciso/security management side of things, social engineering, osint etc" that would have been perfectly fine.

there's a difference between saying something doesn't interest you and suggesting it doesn't matter. i'm pretty sure @LiveOverflow means the former , but the way he tweets makes it pretty easy to interpret it as the latter.
